body_markdown:
## Introduction


In September 2026, Nutanix released a new version of the Nutanix PowerShell cmdlets. This release is designed to provide closer alignment between Nutanix PowerShell automation and the Nutanix v4 APIs.


In today’s article, we’ll explore:


- Installation:


- A brief summary of how to install the latest Nutanix PowerShell Cmdlets on Windows, Ubuntu Linux and Mac OS X.


- Important note: This article assumes you have PowerShell 7.6 or later installed.


- Usage setup:


- How to use built-in Cmdlets to specify Prism Central connection parameters


- Example usage:


- A demonstration script that lists virtual machines using OData-style filters and demonstrates creation of a report configuration


## Prerequisites


Let’s begin by making sure the prerequisites are met.


1. Check the PowerShell version:


```text
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
```


Checking the PowerShell version and confirming version 7.6 or later is installed


1. Verify the PSGallery PowerShell repository is available. This step involves checking the repository, installing the repository if it is NOT installed and, finally, ensuring the repository is trusted.


Important note: This article was tested with PowerShell 7.6 or later. Confirm the supported PowerShell versions for the module release before use.


```text
Get-PSRepository
```


In the screenshot below, the PSGallery repository is installed but is not trusted. If permitted by your organization’s security policy, configure the PowerShell Gallery repository as trusted:


```text
Set-PSRepository -Name PSGallery -InstallationPolicy Trusted
```


Setting the PSGallery to trusted


If the PowerShell Gallery repository is unavailable in your environment, consult your organization’s approved repository configuration process. If appropriate, it can be registered as follows:


```text
Register-PSRepository -Default
```


## Cmdlet Installation


With PowerShell configured for use with the Nutanix Cmdlets, let’s get the Cmdlets installed and carry out our first real tests.


Before continuing, note the following points.


- At the time of publication, the following modules were listed as GA. Verify the status before use.


- ` Nutanix.vmm`
- ` Nutanix.prism`
- ` Nutanix.clustermgmt`
- ` Nutanix.networking`
- ` Nutanix.volumes`
- ` Nutanix.datapolicies`
- ` Nutanix.dataprotection`
- ` Nutanix.licensing`
- ` Nutanix.lifecycle`
- ` Nutanix.microseg` (Nutanix Flow Network Security)
- ` Nutanix.monitoring`
- ` Nutanix.objects`
- ` Nutanix.security`


- Additionally, the following 3 modules have been released with Pre-release, i.e., “Preview”, status (note “Preview” and “Pre-release” refer to the same release status for Nutanix PowerShell Cmdlets).


- ` Nutanix.aiops`
- ` Nutanix.opsmgmt` (NCM Operation Base Platform)
- ` Nutanix.multidomain`


- Lastly, the following module has been released as Preview only:


- ` Nutanix.tenancy`


GA modules are generally intended for production use, subject to the applicable Nutanix support documentation, version compatibility, and environment-specific requirements. Pre-release and Preview modules are subject to change. Consult the applicable Nutanix documentation for support status, and evaluate them in a non-production environment unless production use is expressly supported.


Today, we’ll use the vmm, prism and opsmgmt modules.


### Install the vmm and prism modules


1. In a new PowerShell session, the vmm and prism modules can be installed as follows.


```text
Install-Module -Name Nutanix.Vmm,Nutanix.Prism -Scope CurrentUser
```


Installation of vmm and prism PowerShell modules


Additional modules can be appended to the existing list of installable modules above, if required. By way of example, all currently available GA PowerShell modules could be installed as follows:


```text
Install-Module -Name Nutanix.Prism,Nutanix.Vmm,Nutanix.Clustermgmt,Nutanix.Networking,Nutanix.Volumes,Nutanix.Datapolicies,Nutanix.Dataprotection,Nutanix.Licensing,Nutanix.Lifecycle,Nutanix.Microseg,Nutanix.Monitoring,Nutanix.Objects,Nutanix.Security -Scope CurrentUser
```


Installing all currently available GA PowerShell modules


### Install pre-release opsmgmt module


For modules published with a prerelease designation, use -AllowPrerelease when permitted by the module’s distribution and your organization’s policies. Additionally, the -AllowPrerelease flag allows a single pre-release module to be installed at a time, requiring the use of a PowerShell loop if more than 1 pre-release module is to be installed.


1. Install opsmgmt:


```text
Install-Module -Name Nutanix.opsmgmt -Scope CurrentUser -AllowPrerelease
```


Installation of a single pre-release PowerShell module:` opsmgmt`


As mentioned, the -AllowPrerelease flag allows a single pre-release module installation at a time. If required, a PowerShell loop can be used:


```text
'Nutanix.Aiops','Nutanix.Iam','Nutanix.Multidomain','Nutanix.Opsmgmt' | ForEach-Object { Install-Module -Name $_ -Scope CurrentUser -AllowPrerelease }
```


Using a PowerShell loop to install multiple pre-release PowerShell modules with a “single” command


### Verify Installation Status


With the Nutanix PowerShell Cmdlets installed and not showing any obvious errors, it can be a good idea to manually verify the installation status.


```text
Get-Module -ListAvailable Nutanix.* | Select-Object Name, Version
```


Verifying PowerShell Cmdlet install status


## Cmdlet Structure


Following the naming conventions that may be familiar to current PowerShell Cmdlet users, the new Nutanix PowerShell Cmdlets are named in a way that clearly defines their purpose.


- ` Get-<hypervisor><module><resource><operation>`
- ` Set-<hypervisor><module><resource><operation>`


Practical examples:


- ` Get-AhvConfigVmById`
- ` Set-AhvConfigVmById`


## Prism Central Connection


Before using the Nutanix PowerShell Cmdlets to interact with Prism Central, appropriate credentials and endpoint information must be available. A practical example:


- Prism Central IP address:` 10.0.0.1` , represented by` $pc_ip` in the demo scripts
- Username:` admin`
- Password: Collected at runtime


In a production environment, credentials should not be hard-coded into any script or file that could compromise the environment’s security. With this in mind, the demo scripts collect credential information as follows:


```text
$Credential = Get-Credential -UserName $username -Message "Prism Central credentials"
```


After entering an appropriate password for the` admin` user, the Prism Central connection instance can be created and re-used.


Note:` -SkipCertificateCheck` disables TLS certificate validation. Use it only in a controlled test environment where the risk is understood and approved; do not use it as a general production workaround.


```text
# import the required modules
Import-Module Nutanix.Opsmgmt, Nutanix.Vmm, Nutanix.Prism


# setup the Prism Central configuration
Set-PrismCentralConfig -Host $pc_ip -Username $Credential.UserName -Password $Credential.Password -SkipCertificateCheck
```


## Using the Nutanix PowerShell cmdlets


With the PowerShell modules installed and confirmed available, the next step is to actually use the new Cmdlets. We’ll break this into 2 parts:


1. A simple demo that lists virtual machines based on a name filter. This part will also configure the Prism Central connection; these steps are near identical in part 2.
2. An end-to-end example script that demonstrates creation of a report configuration.


- The report configuration script is for demo purposes only and should be evaluated for suitability before use in a customer environment.


Rather than walk through every line in each demo, both scripts have been available in the[NutanixDev Code-Samples GitHub Repository](https://github.com/nutanixdev/code-samples/) . See the powershell/v4apis folder for demos specific to the new Cmdlets.


### Part 1: List VMs


The first demo requires the Prism Central IP address and username to be passed as command-line parameters. To ensure no passwords are hard-coded into the demo scripts, the user password will be entered via the` Get-Credential` Cmdlet. Additionally, the` vmm` module will be installed if it is not already available.


With the Prism Central IP address/FQDN and credentials available, the connection instance will be created using the` Set-PrismCentralConfig` Cmdlet. We can re-use this instance throughout the script, if other modules are required that use the same endpoint and credentials.


Lastly, we’ll define the Odata filter so that only powered-off VMs are included, the list will be requested using the new` Get-AhvConfigVmsList` Cmdlet, and a simple summary returned to the user.


The script can now be run as follows:


```text
./list_vms_powered_off.ps1 -pc_ip <pc_ip_or_fqdn> -username <username>
```


Nutanix Cmdlets for PowerShell demo: Build filtered list of powered-off virtual machines


In the demo environment used for this example, the query returned 2 powered-off VMs.


### **Part 2: Generate Report Configuration**


In part 2, a Prism Central report configuration will be generated using the` Nutanix.Opsmgmt` module.


**IMPORTANT NOTE** : Some features previously accessed through Prism Central may be available through the Intelligent Operations app in Nutanix Cloud Manager, depending on the environment and software version. To keep this demo simple, this script assumes the target environment has **NOT** migrated to Next-Gen Nutanix Cloud Manager. To use this demo in an environment that **HAS** migrated to Next-Gen Nutanix Cloud Manager, the` Set-PrismCentralConfig` Cmdlet will need to have the` -Port 443` flag added. In the tested configuration, the Cmdlet used port 9440 by default. Confirm the endpoint and port requirements for the specific module, Prism Central, and Nutanix Cloud Manager versions in use.


` -SkipCertificateCheck` disables TLS certificate validation. Use it only in a controlled test environment where the risk is understood and approved; do not use it as a general production workaround.


For example:


```text
Set-PrismCentralConfig -Host $pc_ip -Port 443 -Username $Credential.UserName -Password $Credential.Password -SkipCertificateCheck
```


This demo uses the exact same structure in terms of connection preparation, so we’ll skip this part in the explanation. End-to-end, here’s what our report demo script will accomplish, excluding the repeated preparation section.


1. Sets up Prism Central connection credentials
2. Report defaults will be defined:


- The report period start and end dates, if the user does not enter custom values


3. Builds a list of existing report configurations, using the` Get-ConfigReportConfigsList` Cmdlet
4. Requests the default recipient name and email address. Unless otherwise specified, these will be used when the new report configuration generates a report
5. Creates the report Widget instances; in this demo only VM CPU usage will be included in the report
6. Creates the report schedule; in this example, the report configuration is scheduled to run once per year.


#### A Test Run


Now that we understand the report demo’s workflow, let’s take a look at the script in operation. To demonstrate the single required change for environments using Next-Gen Nutanix Cloud Manager, this example sends the request to our demo environment’s NCM endpoint on port 443.


Running the PowerShell Cmdlets demo script and creating a new NCM Report Configuration


The report configuration details were collected, parsed, and applied to a new report configuration.


## Conclusion


The Nutanix PowerShell cmdlets provide another way to work with selected Nutanix v4 API operations. Designed to align PowerShell workflows more closely with selected Nutanix v4 API operations, the cmdlets can help users transition from earlier automation approaches.


Both code samples in this article can be downloaded from the NutanixDev PowerShell Code Samples repository:


- [List VMs](https://www.nutanix.dev/code_samples/new-powershell-cmdlets-list-vms/)
- [Generate Report Config](https://www.nutanix.dev/code_samples/new-powershell-cmdlets-generate-report-config/)
